title: Rolling rotis
hookLine: kneading and rolling bread in the langar is seva with dough

cards: Sunday morning in the back of a busy gurdwara kitchen: the smell of flour and hot iron. Around a low table, a circle of women and men sit on the floor with rolling pins. One pinches off balls of dough.
The next flattens them. The next rolls them into circles, with a little flick after every push.

Nearby, someone flips them on a huge, flat iron griddle, then onto the open flame for a second, where they puff up like small balloons. Flour on everyone's arms. Gossip, laughter, a shabad playing on someone's phone.
And a stack of rotis growing taller by the minute.

teach.b: Roti is the simple flatbread at the center of a Punjabi meal, and at the center of langar too. In many gurdwaras the langar rotis are called prashada, the same word used for something received as a blessing.
So the bread isn't just food. It's something given.

teach.h: ALL THREE SEVAS IN ONE BREAD.
teach.b: Rolling rotis is seva with dough, and it uses all three of the sevas you met: the hands knead and roll, the mind teaches the new person how to turn the circle, and the flour itself may be bought with daswandh, the tenth that Sikhs give.
It's a good place to learn, too. Grandmothers teach teenagers.

Beginners make lopsided shapes, and nobody minds, because a lopsided roti tastes the same. In the biggest kitchens, like the Harmandir Sahib's, machines now help, but volunteers still roll by hand beside them.
Think back to the bread in the stories. On day thirty-three, Guru Nanak chose the coarse bread of Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned it honestly, over the rich feast of a man who didn't.

On day forty-six, Mata Khivi ran the kitchen at Khadur, and tradition remembers her langar for its care and its warmth. In these stories, bread carries the honesty of whoever earned it and the love of whoever made it.
Roll a roti in langar and you join a long line: Lalo, Khivi, and every volunteer since.

how: Volunteers in gurdwara kitchens knead, roll and cook rotis for langar, often sitting together on the floor; newcomers are welcome to learn, and in the largest kitchens machines help alongside hand-rolling.

games.q: you're new in the langar kitchen. your first roti comes out shaped like a map of somewhere. what happens?
o: it goes on the stack with the others.
games.why: a lopsided roti tastes the same. rolling rotis is a place to learn, and grandmothers teach beginners as they go.

practice: If you have bread nearby, a roti, a slice, a cracker, hold it in your hands; if not, picture one, warm from the pan.
Think of all the hands behind it: whoever grew the wheat, milled the flour, mixed the dough, baked it, drove it, sold it.
Then picture one person you could share it with, and see yourself tearing it in two and handing them the bigger half.

wordCard.voice: Rolling rotis. The seva of making langar's bread by hand, called prashada in many gurdwaras: something given, not just food.
